61	## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them
62	
63	**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. Nothing here is irreversible.
64	
65	**Push and open pull requests freely. Kent merges** — or asks the coordinator to, as he did for all of stack 03; then use §5. Never merge without being asked.
66	
67	**All sub-agents run on Opus.** Kent said so directly. Do not downgrade a sub-agent to save tokens.
68	
69	**Decisions come before code.** A significant architectural choice needs a decision record (`docs/adr/`, next number **0015**, copy `template.md`). Write it `proposed`, ask Kent, build only after he accepts. Small tooling choices already covered by a record need no new one.
70	
71	**How to ask him — this worked.** Collect the open questions; have a read-only Opus agent analyse them for *the most principled, simplest-to-maintain design, balanced against functionality*, sorting them into "needs Kent" and "falls out of something already decided"; then put the first group to him with the **question tool**: each in plain words with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, the recommended option first. He settled eleven questions and approved fourteen small ones in one sitting. Record the answers in a dated note under `plans/notes/` and fold them into the chapters the same day.
72	
73	**Two things Kent will veto on sight.**
74	1. **A template-looking interface.** Default component-library styling, a spinner followed by a dump of results, pop-up dialogs, a tangled hairball graph. His first reaction to the first canvas was "closer to spare than rich" — density and deliberate detail are wanted.
75	2. **Not knowing why it did that.** Any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source. This applies to the product *and* to your own work: a number nobody computed is never typed by hand — not in a fixture, not in a chapter, not in a test.
76	
77	**Write plainly.** No unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.
78	
79	**The spec is a book; decision records are a journal.** Do not number spec files. A journal entry's measurements are dated facts — add a dated note rather than rewriting them; a book chapter is kept true.
80	
81	**Authority stays with Kent.** Offer options with a recommendation; do not argue him into things. If you take a call on his behalf, say so, say why, and make it easy to overturn. Questions go at the bottom of `STATUS.md` under "Waiting on Kent" **and in chat**, because he does not read `plans/` unprompted.

85	## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)
86	
87	- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
88	- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
89	- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
90	- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
91	- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**
92	
93	### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is
94	
95	When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.
96	
97	### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)
98	
99	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:
100	
101	```bash
102	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
103	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
104	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
105	```
106	
107	After a parent merges:
108	
109	1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
110	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
111	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
112	   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
113	3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
114	4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
115	5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

140	## 7. The worktree pattern
141	
142	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
143	
144	- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
145	- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
146	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
147	- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
148	- Remove worktrees after the merge.

152	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
153	
154	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
155	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
156	3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
157	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
158	5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
159	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
160	7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
161	8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
162	9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
163	10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
164	11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
165	12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
166	13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
167	15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
168	16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
169	17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
170	18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
171	19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
172	20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
173	21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
174	22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost about fifty-two minutes that day (twice in full, a third time to five runs of twenty) and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
175	23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
176	24. **A defect an agent "fixed" without a browser is a hypothesis — revert the fix and watch the test go red before believing either.** Stack 04's polish branch boasted that its new layout check *"found its first defect before it was ever run"*: three fields overflowing the panel. With both "fixes" reverted the fields still sat inside it — `width: 100%` had always been there — and the check written to catch the overflow could not have seen one (the panel scrolls sideways, so scrolling a field into view made it measure as inside). Four deliberate breakages through the queue settled both in ten minutes.
177	25. **Anything paid is kept OUTSIDE the worktree that ran it.** `KATALYST_RUNS=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/.runs`. The raw run behind the committed Hormuz recording died with a removed worktree, and `docs/measurements.md` has to say so. And a program that writes its kept run only when a case ENDS loses it to a hard kill.
178	26. **Before writing "X says why", open X.** In one evening the coordinator wrote that a scorecard row named its effort (it did not — only the kept run did) and glossed a stop reason from its name (`width_cap` is not "the map reached its widest"). Both were caught only by looking. A sentence about what a file holds is a claim like any other.
179	27. **The suite had never met a live run, a keyed first screen, or a generated map — and Kent met all three in his first five minutes.** Every browser test plays a recording at 0.4 s an event, with an empty key, over the one curated map where every number exists. So a dead `?` key, a minute of silence after pressing *Watch it build*, a recording unreachable with a key, and 36 empty cells of 54 on the tiles were all invisible to 1 000 green tests. **Walk the product the way its owner will — with the key in, on a map nobody curated — before calling a stack done.** And when analysts plan the fix, put what the owner literally asked for on the table at full strength beside their alternative: three of four had quietly argued him out of it, and an adversarial pass re-counted their ~12 sessions at ~25.
180	14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

#!/bin/bash
# heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>
#
# The one queue for anything heavy on this machine: a whole test suite, a browser
# run, a repeat bar. It waits its turn, runs the command, and gives the turn back.
# One at a time, whoever asks. Last session three or four suites ran together, the
# load sat at 20-23, and the load itself caused "flaky" failures that then had to
# be chased (STATUS 2026-09-21).
#
# The turn is a directory (making one is atomic). It holds the owner's process id,
# so a turn left behind by a killed run is taken back rather than waited on for ever.
#
# NOT for a single test file, a linter or a type check: run those directly.
set -uo pipefail
LOCK=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.lock
LOG=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.log
LABEL=${1:?usage: heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>}; shift
[ "${1:-}" = "--" ] && shift
waited=0
until mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
  owner=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null || echo "")
  if [ -n "$owner" ] && ! kill -0 "$owner" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "heavy: taking back a turn left by dead process $owner ($(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null))" >&2
    rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
  fi
  [ $((waited % 60)) -eq 0 ] && echo "heavy: '$LABEL' waiting behind '$(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null)' (${waited}s)" >&2
  sleep 5; waited=$((waited + 5))
done
echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid"; echo "$LABEL" > "$LOCK/label"
trap 'rm -rf "$LOCK"' EXIT
start=$(date +%s)
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') START $LABEL (waited ${waited}s, load $(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2}'))" >> "$LOG"
"$@"; code=$?
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') END   $LABEL exit=$code took=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s" >> "$LOG"
exit $code

#!/bin/bash
# land.sh <pr> <title> <message-file>
# GitHub restacks a child branch onto main by itself when its parent merges, so this only:
# checks the base is main and the branch sits on main, waits for the four checks, squash-merges via the async route.
set -euo pipefail
PR=$1; TITLE=$2; MSG=$3
cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst
for i in $(seq 1 12); do BASE=$(gh pr view $PR --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName); [ "$BASE" = "main" ] && break; sleep 5; done
[ "$BASE" = "main" ] || { echo "base is $BASE, not main"; exit 3; }
git fetch -q origin
HEAD_SHA=$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)
git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main $HEAD_SHA || { echo "head $HEAD_SHA does not sit on main yet"; exit 5; }
echo "head ${HEAD_SHA:0:7} sits on main; waiting for checks…"
for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  out=$(gh pr checks $PR 2>&1 || true)
  if echo "$out" | grep -qw "fail"; then echo "CHECK FAILED:"; echo "$out"; exit 4; fi
  if ! echo "$out" | grep -qw "pending" && [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -cw pass)" -ge 4 ]; then break; fi
  sleep 10
done
gh pr checks $PR | awk '{print $1"="$2}' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
[ "$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)" = "$HEAD_SHA" ] || { echo "head moved while waiting"; exit 6; }
